Shu-Fai Cheung--
     I am not an expert (and I would defer to well pretty much anyone) but I most often hear
lah-vahhn'
Some European languages include words that have the same kind of structure as "lavaan," particularly the double a, which, to me, seems to call for emphasis.  Hence, it seems "natural" to accent the second syllable, but render all of the "a"s as "ah" ( as in the Thai monetary unit "baht" or the vowel sound in "what") rather than as the long "a" sound as in "slate" or even as the short "a" sound as in "cat".
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to pronounce it?
parts: I would like to follow suit with the pronunciation of "latent variable analysis", which means, lavaan should pronounce  /'leɪveən/.

I disagree.  This follows the tradition of ANOVA, from the first letters of ANalysis Of VAriance, yet is pronounced "AN oh vuh" or "uh NOH vuh".  No one pronounces it "uh NUH vay" (actually, not possible to pronounce the last syllable like it appears in the word "variance", where the "a" is pronounced the "R-controlled" way).  When an abbreviation becomes its own word, it can be pronounced however it makes sense as it is spelled.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
